source: Dorst & Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution. Design Studies 22(5):425-437
finding: Protocol studies of nine experienced industrial designers, each doing a modest realistic design task. Their concepts were rated by a panel for overall quality and for aspects including creativity. The authors link creativity to how the problem is formulated and to originality, and say the data confirm the co-evolution model of problem and solution spaces. They propose 'default' and 'surprise' problem/solution spaces as refinements.
numbers: N=9 designers; ratings by a panel of experienced educators. Full-text numbers (session length, rating scores) NOT read: the PDF was blocked, only the abstract page (research.tue.nl) was read.
quote: confirm the general validity of the model
limits: Abstract only. Small N, one task, one lab tradition (Delft protocol data). 'Confirmed' means the pattern fits, not that it was tested against a rival model.
agent_relevance: Founding empirical claim behind our S2<->S3 loop: restating the problem should happen after trying solutions, not only before.

source: Cross (2024 chapter) Creative Cognition in Design II: Co-evolution of Problem and Solution (reprint of the 1998 Heron Island workshop paper with Dorst)
finding: Same nine-designer data. The chapter adds a key amendment: in creative design the solution space may be structured BEFORE the problem space, for example when the designer applies prior knowledge of precedents. The model is confirmed but its direction is not fixed.
numbers: Nine experienced industrial designers; solution concepts assessed by a panel of experienced educators.
quote: structuring the solution space prior to the problem space ... rather than the other way around
limits: Abstract page only. Original workshop paper dates from 1998.
agent_relevance: Supports letting the agent start from a known solution pattern (precedent) and then derive the problem frame, not only problem first.

source: Maher & Poon (1996) Modelling design exploration as co-evolution. Microcomputer Civil Engineering 11:195-210 (also chapter 'Formalising Design Exploration as Co-Evolution')
finding: First formal co-evolution model of design. A genetic algorithm normally scores a population of solutions against a fixed fitness function (search with a preset goal). Here the requirements and the solutions evolve together, so the fitness function changes over time. Two implementations are described: a combined-gene approach (requirements and solution in one genotype) and a separate-spaces approach (two interacting populations). The combined-gene version was demonstrated on braced-frame design for buildings.
numbers: No quantitative results in the abstract; 'preliminary results' only, one structural-engineering example.
limits: Abstract page only. Computational demonstration, not a human study. The fitness changes are produced by the algorithm design, not shown to match designers.
agent_relevance: A direct formal template: the scoring rule (our checks) may itself be revised from what the candidate solutions reveal. Conflicts with G3 unless the revision uses held-out evidence.

source: Maher, Poon & Boulanger (2000) A Model of Co-evolutionary Design. Engineering with Computers
finding: Design is modelled as a parallel search for design requirements and for design solutions. Interaction between the two redefines the current fitness function. The authors note that 'fitness' and 'convergence' no longer mean the same thing when the fitness function moves. A second issue is the coupling between the two search spaces. Demonstrated on structural system layout.
numbers: None in abstract.
quote: the interaction between requirements and solution redefine the current fitness function
limits: Abstract page only. Convergence is not guaranteed once the target moves.
agent_relevance: Warns that a moving target can fail to converge. Our program needs a budget and a stop rule for reframing.

source: Maher & Poon (2002 chapter) Adapting Problem Specifications and Design Solutions Using Co-evolution
finding: States the observation behind the model: creative designers refine and revise requirements at the same time as they propose an evolving series of solutions. Standard genetic algorithms need the criteria changed by hand. In the co-evolutionary model the fitness function changes automatically as problem and solution spaces co-evolve.
numbers: 'Preliminary experimental results' in structural engineering, none given in the abstract.
quote: the fitness function is automatically changed as the problem space and solution space coevolve
limits: Abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Gives the idea of automatic, code-driven criterion revision rather than model-judged revision (fits G1 and G5).

source: Maher & Tang (2003) Co-evolution as a computational and cognitive model of design. Research in Engineering Design 14:47-64
finding: Presents the computational model (two parallel search spaces, each space acts as fitness function for the other) and then a protocol study of human designers looking for co-evolution of problem specifications and solutions. The study concludes co-evolution is a good cognitive model and reports similarities and differences with the computational model.
numbers: Number of designers and episodes NOT read (paywalled; abstract page only).
quote: co-evolutionary design is a good cognitive model of design
limits: Abstract only. Author-defended model tested by its authors.
agent_relevance: Second human-data source for the loop; the differences from the algorithmic model are worth reading if full text becomes available.

source: Cross (2024 chapter) Creative Cognition in Design I: The Creative Leap (reprint of Cross 1997, Design Studies 18(4):427-440)
finding: Case study of one 'creative leap' in a recorded laboratory protocol of a small design team. The leap is reinterpreted as a bridging concept between problem space and solution space, one that satisfies relationships on both sides. Design thinking is called 'appositional': problem and solution are placed side by side and matched.
numbers: One example from one recorded team session.
quote: not so much a 'leap', but more akin to 'bridging' between problem space and solution space
limits: Abstract page only. Single case. Insight reconstructed after the fact.
agent_relevance: Defines the stop condition of the loop: stop when one concept matches the problem frame and the solution at once. Can be checked by code as a joint pass.

source: Kokotovich (2015) A case for reimagining reflection-in-action and co-evolution. IASDR2015 paper 378
finding: Conceptual critique. Argues designers 'muddle through' and co-evolve problem and solution on the fly, bounded by their own experience. Proposes to forestall solution development (hold back P(t+1), S(t), S(t+1)) until a broad, mapped problem space exists, using layered knowledge domains and non-hierarchical mind mapping.
numbers: No new data. 13-page paper. Cites Kokotovich (2008, Design Studies 29(1):49-69) for the empirical support.
quote: forestalling solution development in order to focus on developing a well-considered and comprehensively mapped Problem space first holds immense value
limits: Position paper. The proposed model is a 'new fledgling model', untested. Criticises co-evolution mainly for staying inside one domain of knowledge.
agent_relevance: The critique named in our subfield row. Argues for a problem-mapping phase before S3; this is the opposite of fast solution-probing and needs a test.

source: Kokotovich (2008) Problem analysis and thinking tools: an empirical study of non-hierarchical mind mapping. Design Studies 29(1):49-69, as summarised in Kokotovich (2015)
finding: Reported second-hand (the 2008 paper itself was not opened). In that study, more clearly articulated design issues in the early problem-formulation stage went with design proposals rated more creative and better reasoned. Non-hierarchical mind mapping in problem formulation was linked to higher-rated proposals.
numbers: Not given in the 2015 summary: no N, no effect size.
limits: Second-hand summary by the same author. Correlational as summarised. Issue count may be a marker of designer skill, not a cause.
agent_relevance: The only empirical support offered for 'map the problem first'. Treat as [S] single source until the 2008 numbers are read.

source: Storm, van Maanen & Goncalves (2019) Reframing the design process: integrating goals, methods and manifestation into the co-evolution model. ICED19
finding: Two-part study. Part 1: two expert designers interviewed (over 25 years each); they confirmed problem and solution spaces and co-evolution transitions in practice. Added three elements to the model: goal, methods, manifestation (externalising thought). Part 2: 21 bachelor students had a 2-hour workshop; 9 of them in 4 groups were interviewed 3 weeks later. Before the model students treated the problem as fixed once defined.
numbers: Interviews: 2 experts, about 200 codes, about 15 categories, 7 themes. Students: 21 at workshop, 9 interviewed (4 groups of 2-3). 5 of 9 said they became more confident; all said they spent more time reframing (self-report).
quote: the sooner you start designing [entering the solution space], the sooner you discover the problem
limits: Self-report and notebooks, no inter-rater agreement calculated, no control group, group interviews, small N. Authors say validation with expert teams is future work.
agent_relevance: Practical failure mode: novices freeze the problem frame once written. An agent that keeps the frame fixed after S2 repeats this.

source: Storm et al. (2019), citing Wiltschnig, Christensen & Ball (2013) Collaborative problem-solution co-evolution in creative design. Design Studies 34(5)
finding: Second-hand through Storm 2019: co-evolution episodes were shown in design TEAMS, and most solution attempts happened inside co-evolution episodes. The 2013 paper itself was blocked.
numbers: 84% of the team's solution attempts occurred within co-evolution episodes (as quoted by Storm et al., 2019).
limits: Number read only through a secondary citation. Single team, per Storm's description. Full paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Suggests most useful solution generation is tied to frame-shift episodes, so frame updates should be allowed right inside S3.

source: Storm et al. (2019), citing Christiaans (1992) and Akin & Akin (1996)
finding: Second-hand. Christiaans (1992): time spent reflecting on the problem in the first part of the process related to the creativity of the result in design students. Akin & Akin (1996): setting frames of reference and, more importantly, breaking them are ingredients of sudden insight. These cut in two directions: early problem time helps, and frame breaking helps.
numbers: None given in the secondary source.
quote: a relationship was found between the time spent reflecting on the problem in the first part of the design process and the creativity of the result
limits: Quote is Storm et al.'s quote of Christiaans. Originals not opened. Correlation only.
agent_relevance: The only quantitative-style support (via secondary) for spending early effort on the problem. Pair with a09 as the 'map first' side.

source: Cash, Goncalves & Dorst (2023) Method in their madness: explaining how designers think and act through the cognitive co-evolution model. Design Studies 88:101219
finding: Title and metadata only (the page was blocked, 403). It is an open-access (CC BY) extension of co-evolution to a model tying thinking and acting, with Dorst as coauthor.
numbers: 28 citations per Semantic Scholar at time of check.
limits: Content not read. Do not cite findings from it.
agent_relevance: Priority item to read if access opens: it links co-evolution to acting and method use.

source: Martinec, Skec, Horvat & Storga (2020) Revisiting problem-solution co-evolution in the context of team conceptual design activity. Applied Sciences 10(18):6303
finding: Protocol analysis of team ideation and concept review. Tests three assumption sets from standard models: how analysis/synthesis/evaluation map onto problem vs solution space; dominant sequences; the nature of transitions between spaces. Finds inconsistent definitions of analysis, synthesis and evaluation across the literature, and co-evolution patterns that conventional models cannot describe. Analysis-synthesis cycles are important in both divergent (co-evolution) and convergent (refinement) phases. Models the growth in number of new problem and solution entities over the conceptual phase.
numbers: Counts not in abstract (page was blocked; abstract read via Crossref).
quote: co-evolution patterns, which cannot be described by the conventional models
limits: Abstract only. Team data; coding scheme choice drives results.
agent_relevance: Suggests new problem facts keep appearing through the whole generate phase, so a single front-loaded S2 is not enough. Count new problem entities per round as a cheap signal.

source: Halstrom & Galle (2015) Design as co-evolution of problem, solution, and audience. Artifact 3(4)
finding: Theory review. Says co-evolution has merit for understanding design deliberation but leaves practitioners without guidance in some respects. Proposes 'triple co-evolution' that adds the audience of the artifact, using constitutive rhetoric (design offers an audience a subject position).
numbers: None; small sample of design cases.
limits: Conceptual, case examples only.
agent_relevance: Third space: the user or asker. For an agent, the asker's intent may also need updating by the answer; low priority.

source: Feast (2024) Three's company: situation-problem-solution co-evolution. DRS2024
finding: Longitudinal study of 4 MSc student design teams on an industrial design project. Data: observations, interviews, field notes, documents; analysed by visual mapping and temporal bracketing. Some teams that used effectuation pivoted by co-evolving the situation, problem and solution spaces at once.
numbers: 4 teams. No effect sizes.
quote: triadic co-evolution of situation, problem, and solution
limits: Abstract page only. Exploratory, 4 teams, no control.
agent_relevance: Adds the situation (what resources and context exist) as a third thing to update; relevant to tool or budget limits in our schema.

source: Biskjaer, Halskov & de Rooij (2026) Problem-solution co-evolution research in the DRS conference community (2001-2025). DRS2026
finding: Scoping review of the model's use in DRS proceedings. Corpus is 16 papers. Problem and solution spaces are treated as distinct and interdependent. Co-evolution is studied through cognitive, social and systemic lenses. Suggested next steps: design-space visualisation, co-evolution as a flexible boundary concept, and psychological creativity work on problem construction.
numbers: 16 papers from 25 years of DRS conferences.
limits: One conference series only. Review reports use, not effect size. It calls co-evolution a 'flexible boundary concept', i.e. loosely defined.
agent_relevance: Warns the construct is loosely defined, so our version must be operational (what is counted as a frame update) to be testable.

source: Chen, Zhao, Rong, Li & Bei (2023) Comparing the design cognitive process between problem-driven and solution-driven industrial design students. Int J Technol Des Educ 33:557-584
finding: Uses the P-S index from the Function-Behavior-Structure ontology to split 54 students into problem-driven and solution-driven. Problem-driven students repeatedly state problem items; solution-driven students develop solution structure with high generate-solution intensity. The classification stayed fairly stable across experimental conditions. A constraint condition raised the process intensity of solution-driven students but acted more complexly for problem-driven ones.
numbers: N=54 participants, two groups; exact group sizes and statistics not read (abstract page only).
quote: design cognitive classifications of ID students had relative stability
limits: Abstract only. Students, not experts. The two styles are traits, so the finding that they are stable argues co-evolution style differs by person.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable P-S index we could compute on agent traces: the share of steps about problem vs solution.

source: Kruger & Cross (2006) Solution driven versus problem driven design: strategies and outcomes. Design Studies 27(5):527-548
finding: Known from background only; the paper was blocked and no abstract was read. It compares design strategies (problem-driven vs solution-driven, among others) with the rated quality of the outcome, using protocol data on a design task. Exact results are not recorded here because they were not read.
numbers: Not read. 206 citations per Crossref.
limits: Do not use as evidence until opened. Listed so the next pass reads it: it directly tests the 'problem first versus solution first' question.
agent_relevance: The most direct outcome test of problem-driven vs solution-driven order. High priority to open.

source: Suwa, Gero & Purcell (2000) Unexpected discoveries and S-invention of design requirements. Design Studies 21(6)
finding: Title and metadata only. The title states the idea: unexpected discoveries made while sketching lead designers to invent new requirements (problem items) during the process.
numbers: 222 citations per Crossref. No data read.
limits: Content not read.
agent_relevance: Mechanism for how problem items get created: from surprises in the solution artefact. Matches our rule G2 (revise from real output).

source: Guo, Yin, Sun & Chen (2024) Empirical study of problem-solution co-evolution in human-GAI collaborative conceptual design. DRS2024
finding: Retrospective protocol analysis of the verbal reasoning of 20 novice designers co-designing with generative AI (text-to-text and text-to-image models). Creativity assessments show GAI can amplify team creativity by fostering human abductive reasoning. Proposes a human-GAI co-evolution model where the AI aids problem-framing exploration, with 'introspection' and 'retrospection' as key constructs.
numbers: N=20 novice designers. Effect sizes not in the abstract.
quote: GAI has the potential to amplify team creativity by fostering human abductive reasoning
limits: Abstract page only. Novices, retrospective protocol (memory-based), human-AI team not an autonomous LLM. 'Potential' wording.
agent_relevance: The only LLM-involved co-evolution protocol study found: the benefit came through the human reframing the problem, not the model doing it.

source: Lim & Lee (2025) Impact of the visual fidelity of externalized ideas on participants' cognitive actions and co-evolution: generative AI-supported multidisciplinary co-design. IASDR 2025
finding: Multidisciplinary co-design workshop with pre/post surveys, video protocol analysis of utterances and post-interviews. Tests how GAI-made, higher-fidelity visualisations of ideas change cognitive actions, co-evolution and knowledge exchange. Proposes strategies to use GAI to make idea representations concrete.
numbers: Sample sizes and statistics not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract page only. Results not visible; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Fits the manifestation idea in a10: a concrete externalised draft triggers frame changes. Suggests S3 outputs should be made concrete enough to expose conflicts.

source: Chen et al. (2025) GPSdesign: Integrating generative AI with a problem-solution co-evolution network to support product conceptual design. Int J Human-Computer Interaction
finding: Title and metadata only (publisher page blocked). It is a tool that combines generative AI with a problem-solution co-evolution network for conceptual design, 12 citations per Crossref.
numbers: None read.
limits: Content not read, results unknown.
agent_relevance: Closest direct build of the idea in an LLM tool; open next to see measured gains.

source: O'Hara (2025) Agentic architecture mediation for LLM assistants: preventing solution-jumping with requirements elicitation. TechRxiv preprint
finding: Says LLM assistants often show 'solution-jumping': they accept a user's technology choice (e.g. Kubernetes) without validating requirements. A multi-agent Five Whys requirements workflow plus a deterministic evaluation engine steers toward requirements-first reasoning. Splits duties: LLM for dialogue, deterministic code for evaluation.
numbers: 6 industry antipatterns tested; 100% detection of solution mismatches; average cost about $0.01 per session.
limits: Abstract only. Preprint, only 6 cases, authors' own tests, detection is not the same as better final answers.
agent_relevance: Evidence the opposite failure exists for LLMs: jumping to solutions. Supports a problem-check before S3, with the check done by code (G5).

source: Hu, Woods, Zhang, Li & Li (2026) Framing the fuzzy: mapping expert designers' problem framing through C-K theory. DRS2026
finding: Interviews and real-time framing tasks with 12 expert designers (5+ years). Visual mapping and temporal bracketing show three experience-mediated reasoning modes that alternate between exploration and consolidation, using Concept (C) and Knowledge (K) spaces.
numbers: N=12 experts, 3 reasoning modes.
limits: Abstract page only. Qualitative.
agent_relevance: Expert framing alternates exploring and consolidating; supports an explicit explore/consolidate switch driven by a signal, not a fixed order.

source: Gong et al. (2026) How LLM-based agents shape engineering design thinking: a qualitative study with undergraduate software engineering students. ASEE 2026
finding: Title only (publisher page blocked). A qualitative study of how LLM agents affect design thinking in software engineering undergraduates.
numbers: None read.
limits: Content not read.
agent_relevance: Possible source of student-with-LLM evidence on problem framing; unread.

source: Kopecka, Santema & Buijs (2012) Designerly ways of muddling through. J Business Research 65(6):729-739, as cited by Kokotovich (2015)
finding: Second-hand. Compares design thinking with 'disjointed incrementalism' (muddling through), where change is made in small steps that fail to consider larger context issues. Kokotovich uses this to argue co-evolution is incremental and domain-bounded.
numbers: None.
limits: Original not opened; used only as the source of the 'muddle through' critique.
agent_relevance: Names the risk: a loop of small local fixes never questions the frame. Our impasse operator must be able to widen the frame.

source: Access note for this pass (Angle A)
finding: Search quota was used up (WebSearch), arXiv and Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429, OpenAlex had no budget, and publisher PDFs (ScienceDirect, MDPI, ASEE, tandfonline, ORO, UTS repository for Dorst and Cross) returned 403 or Cloudflare pages. Only Crossref metadata, Springer and DRS abstract pages, Kokotovich full text and Storm et al. full text could be read.
numbers: Full texts read: 2 (Kokotovich 2015; Storm et al. 2019). Abstract pages read: about 14.
limits: Dorst & Cross 2001 results (session length, ratings, counts of problem/solution transitions) are NOT recorded here. Another pass with PDF access is needed.
agent_relevance: Treat all items here as [S] or lower until the full texts of a01, a06, a11, a19 are read.
